questions.knowledge_point: Express Surface Integrals as Repeated Integrals
questions.problem:
Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}yz,$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=-x+y$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-x+y)=-1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-x+y)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(-1)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}y(-x+y)\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\sqrt{3}(-{x}^{3}y+{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2}xyz,$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=-\sqrt{2}x-\sqrt{2}y$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{2}x-\sqrt{2}y)=-\sqrt{2},
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\sqrt{2}x-\sqrt{2}y)=-\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(-\sqrt{2})}^{2}+{(-\sqrt{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{2}xy(-\sqrt{2}x-\sqrt{2}y)\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(-2{x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2})\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,-2\sqrt{5}({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}z,$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\boxed{}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(-2x)}^{2}+{(-2y)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}{y}^{2}(-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,(-{x}^{4}{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}{y}^{4})\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=-2x,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=4y.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(-2x)}^{2}+{(4y)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}(-{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})^{2}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,({x}^{6}-4{y}^{2}{x}^{4}+4{y}^{4}{x}^{2})\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2},$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=y-2x$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $-1\le y\le 1.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\boxed{}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-2x)=-2
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-2x)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(-2)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{6}\,xy(y-2x)^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,\sqrt{6}\,xy(y-2x)^{2}\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}\frac{z}{\sqrt{1+2{cos}^{2}⁡(x+y)}}\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)$ for $0\le x\le \pi $ and $-x\le y\le x.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y),
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y).
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{z}{\sqrt{1+2{cos}^{2}⁡(x+y)}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}{\sqrt{1+2{cos}^{2}⁡(x+y)}}\sqrt{1+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y))^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}{\cancel{\sqrt{1+2{cos}^{2}⁡(x+y)}}}\cancel{\sqrt{1+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y))^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-x}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)]_{y=-x}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[x-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}\frac{z}{36x}\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=4x+8y$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le x.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+8y)=4,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x+8y)=8.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{z}{36x}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{4x+8y}{36x}\sqrt{1+{4}^{2}+{8}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,9\frac{4(x+2y)}{36x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{x+2y}{x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{x}(1+\frac{2y}{x})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{[y+\frac{{y}^{2}}{x}]}_{0}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x}-0)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =[{x}^{2}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =4-1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}\frac{z-y}{\sqrt{6}y}\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=2x+y$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le e.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+y)=2,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{z-y}{\sqrt{6}y}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{(2x+y)-y}{\sqrt{6}y}\sqrt{1+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{2x}{y}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{2x}{y}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2x[\operatorname{ln}⁡y]_{y=1}^{y=e}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =[{x}^{2}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =4-1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}({x}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=5x-y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2x.$

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=\frac{1}{4}+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $-2\le y\le 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{4}+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{4}+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{z}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{xy}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{xy}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{2xy}{\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{2xy}{\cancel{\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}}}\cancel{\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{1}(2xy)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[x{y}^{2}]_{y=-2}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}(1-0) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066807/assets/5d6cedcc2d8c5a232d8d7ed89f050fa7a545ed0da6075ddb44eec67e065b9e87.png)

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}3{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=-4x+\sqrt{8}y$ and whose domain is the upper half-circle of radius $1$ centered at $O$, as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4x+\sqrt{8}y)=-4,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4x+\sqrt{8}y)=\sqrt{8}.
$$

 

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}3{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3{x}^{2}y\cdot \sqrt{1+(-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{8})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3{x}^{2}y\cdot \sqrt{25}\,\text{d}A \\  & =5{∬}_{D}\,3{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}5{∬}_{D}\,3{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A & =5{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =5{∬}_{Δ}3{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =15{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =15{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =15{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{[\frac{{r}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[-{cos}^{3}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∬}_{S}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=x+\sqrt{3}y$ whose domain is the circle of radius $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+\sqrt{3}y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+\sqrt{3}y)=\sqrt{3}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{5}{∬}_{D}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{∬}_{D}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =\sqrt{5}{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{∬}_{Δ}{e}^{({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{∬}_{Δ}{e}^{{r}^{2}}r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}r{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{e}^{{r}^{2}}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{{e}^{4}-1}{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}({e}^{4}-1)}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}({e}^{4}-1)}{2}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\sqrt{5}({e}^{4}-1)\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066807/assets/d19d54d0e76ced24d1bd9f865578b72f2b8d67414c8506499c6ae7b1300a6275.png)

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}(x+y)\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=-2x+2y$ and whose domain is the left half-circle of radius $1$ centered at $O$, as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2x+2y)=-2,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2x+2y)=2.
$$

 

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}(x+y)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)\cdot \sqrt{1+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)\cdot \sqrt{9}\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{∬}_{D}\,(x+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{∬}_{D}\,(x+y)\,\text{d}A & =3{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =3{∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}8xy\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=y-2x$ and whose domain is the quarter-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O$ in the first quadrant, as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-2x)=-2,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-2x)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}8xy\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}8xy\cdot \sqrt{1+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}8xy\cdot \sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{D}\,8xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6}{∬}_{D}\,8xy\,\text{d}A & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{Δ}8r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{Δ}4{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}4{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta [{r}^{4}]_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}16\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =8\sqrt{6}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =8\sqrt{6}(1+1) \\  & =16\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=xz,$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=x^2-y$ for $0 \leq x \leq 2$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066807/assets/e44b57bad88dcc1c13680f0e8f110696c6975b16c1d9553138fb6aeb4cadb8f9.png)

What is the missing expression?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2-y) = 2x,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^2-y) = -1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(2x)}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,x({x}^{2}-y)\sqrt{2+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,({x}^{3}-xy)\sqrt{2+4{x}^{2}}\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is ${\color{blue} (x^3-xy) \sqrt{2+4x^2}}.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{z-x+y^2}} \: \textrm{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=1+x+y^2$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $-1 \leq y \leq 1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(1+x+y^2\right) = 1,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(1+x+y^2\right) = 2y.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{z-x+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{(1+x+{y}^{2})-x+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2(1+2{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{1+2{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot (1-(-1)) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot 2 \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{S} x^2y \: \textrm{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=\sqrt2x-y$ and whose domain is a semicircle of radius $1$ centered at $O$ in the upper-half plane, as shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(\sqrt2x-y) = \sqrt2,
$$

and

$$
\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(\sqrt2x-y) = -1.
$$

 

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\cdot \sqrt{1+(\sqrt{2})^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\cdot \sqrt{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A & =2{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,[\frac{{r}^{5}}{5}]_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{2}{15}{[-{cos}^{3}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{2}{15}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{4}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$
